title: How to Market Your Barbershop on Instagram
summary: Most barbershops use Instagram as a portfolio. Here's how to turn your profile into a booking engine that fills chairs. A complete guide for shop owners.
body_text: Your Instagram is probably your shop's strongest marketing asset. It's also probably not driving as many bookings as it could. Most shops have the content side figured out: great cuts, a growing following, consistent posts. What's missing is the conversion layer: the path that takes someone from scrolling to a confirmed appointment. Instagram is one of the most effective client acquisition channels available to shop owners right now. But most shops treat it as a digital portfolio instead of a booking engine. This guide gives you the system: what to post, how often, and how to close the gap between the scroll and the chair. For a broader look at filling your calendar, see our barbershop marketing tips guide . Set Your Profile Up for Discovery Before you post anything, your profile has to work. Instagram uses your Name field (the bold text below your profile photo) as a local search signal. When someone in your city searches "barber near me" or "fade specialist in Houston," this field is one of the things Instagram checks. Don't put a slogan there. Put what your shop does and where it is. Something like: "King Cutz | Houston Barbershop" or "Downtown Cuts | Fades + Beards, Atlanta." Clear beats clever here. Your bio follows the same logic. Four lines: What your shop specializes in Your city or neighborhood A trust signal (years open, number of barbers, any signature services) A direct instruction: "Book below" or "Tap to grab your spot" And your link in bio should go directly to your booking calendar. One tap. No detours. What to Post (Most Shops Get This Wrong) The most common mistake: posting only finished cuts. Finished cuts matter, but they're one piece of a system. Here's the content mix that builds a following and actually fills a calendar. Transformation content. Before-and-after. The visual payoff. This drives saves and shares, which signals to the algorithm that your content is worth spreading. Aim for two or three per week. Process content. A 15-second clip of a fade in progress. The cleanup on a beard line. Seeing the work up close is more convincing to a first-time client than seeing the end result alone. Availability content. Direct and low-pressure. "Two spots open Tuesday. Link in bio." This is the type of content that converts passive followers into confirmed bookings. Most shops underuse it. Culture content. Your shop, your team, the atmosphere. Clients don't just book a haircut. They book an experience. Show them what yours feels like. Reels vs. Static Posts Short answer: Reels reach new people. Static posts keep your grid sharp for first impressions. Instagram is heavily weighted toward Reels right now. A 20-second transformation Reel will reach significantly more people than the same cut posted as a photo. If you're not posting Reels, you're giving up reach to shops that are. That said, your grid still matters. When someone lands on your profile for the first time, those first nine squares are how they decide whether to follow or book. Mix both. For Reels: keep them 7 to 20 seconds. Start mid-cut. Don't open on setup. Add a text overlay with the cut type and your city. Keep captions direct and always include a booking call to action. How Often to Post Consistency matters more than volume. Three solid posts a week, every week, will outperform a burst of ten posts followed by two weeks of silence. Instagram rewards accounts that show up on a schedule. Going dark loses reach, and rebuilding it takes longer than maintaining it. A sustainable starting cadence for a shop: 3 Reels per week (transformations, process clips, availability) Stories 4 to 5 days per week 1 static post per week Stories are underused by most shops. They're how your existing followers see you daily, not just when a post hits their feed. Post your open slots there. Respond to replies. Stories build the ongoing touchpoint that brings clients back every few weeks. That kind of consistency is what builds a client retention system that compounds over time. Turning a Profile Visit into a Booking This is where the money gets left on the table. A client can love your content, visit your profile, and still never book, because the path from "I want this" to "I'm confirmed" has too many steps or sends them somewhere confusing. Angel, a shop owner using SQUIRE, described the standard her shop holds: "Once they hit that link in bio, they can book right there." That's what the experience should feel like. One tap from your profile to a live booking calendar. No form to fill out. No DM chain. No call-back required. SQUIRE's Instagram booking integration connects your link in bio directly to your shop's booking page. A client finds you, likes what they see, and books in under a minute. See how Instagram booking works with SQUIRE What to Stop Doing A few patterns that hurt more than they help. Posting cuts with no hook. Great work needs context. Add what the client asked for, what you changed, how long it took. Give people a reason to save the post. Using generic hashtags. Tags like #barber and #fade are so oversaturated they give you almost no discoverability. Use city-specific and style-specific tags instead. #AtlantaBarber will reach more of the right people than #Barber ever will. Sending followers somewhere confusing. A bio link that goes to a homepage, a Yelp page, or a dead URL breaks the conversion. Check your link in bio right now. Where does it go? How many taps does it take to book? Going dark for weeks. Even a single Story a day keeps your shop visible to the followers you already have. You don't need a film crew. You need your phone and 30 seconds. FAQs The System, Not the Moment Instagram rewards consistency over perfection. A shop that posts three times a week for six months will outperform one that posts brilliantly for two weeks and disappears. Build the habit: transformation content shows what your shop can do, process content builds trust, availability content drives bookings. Keep your profile optimized, your link pointed straight at your calendar, and your Stories active between posts. That's the difference between a portfolio and a booking engine. title: Trendex arrives in the USA
summary: Trendex arrives in the USA, discover the reasons for this choice and its Implications
body_text: Trendex arrives in the United States The long-awaited arrival of Trendex in the United States is imminent. This platform dedicated to official fan clubs and exclusive experiences, focused on promising talents, established champions, and legends from various sporting and cultural worlds, is poised to make a remarkable entry into the American market. ‍ A Vast Choice of Talents What further sets Trendex apart in the US market is its impressive roster of talent, whom fans can follow and support by joining their official fan clubs. These fan clubs provide access to exclusive content, unique rewards, and community-only experiences. The diversity of talent on Trendex ranges from soccer players to content creators to basketball players. It is the latter who are attracting particular attention from the American public. ‍ Why the United States? By combining entertainment, proximity to talent, and exclusive experiences, Trendex offers a unique approach for sports and culture enthusiasts. The US market shows strong interest in this type of direct relationship between fans and talent, making it a key step in our development. Targeting an English-speaking audience also allows us to broaden our reach and prepare for expansion into other parts of the world. We are motivated by several key objectives: American audience affinity for this type of experience: The American audience is particularly receptive to platforms that strengthen the bond between fans and talent. Trendex is fully in line with this dynamic by offering official fan clubs and engaging experiences. Opening up to a new audience: Entering the US market represents a major opportunity for Trendex to attract new fans and build an international community around the talent featured on the platform. Facilitating openness to the rest of the world: By developing a solid foundation in the United States, Trendex is strengthening its ability to expand internationally and reach an ever-wider audience. Integration of recognized international talent: By welcoming internationally renowned talent, Trendex enriches the fan experience and affirms its position as the go-to platform for official fan clubs and exclusive experiences. To the United States... and beyond! Trendex's expansion into the United States marks a new stage in its global ambitions. After opening up to the Spanish-speaking market with the translation of the app into Spanish, then rolling out in several regions of the Middle East and Italy thanks to collaborations with influencers, Trendex is now exploring new opportunities in several fast-growing Asian markets. ‍ Join Trendex now and be part of an international adventure alongside the talents you admire. ‍

title: When Broken Down in the Boonies, Get Creative and Rely on Community
summary: A good friend of mine is a retired executive with, as expected, strong executive skills. He has applied himself to organizing bi-annual road tours for his small group of car enthusiasts that make a three-day loop up and down the Appalachian Mountains. This has been going on for years, and I was invited to join […]
body_text: A good friend of mine is a retired executive with, as expected, strong executive skills. He has applied himself to organizing bi-annual road tours for his small group of car enthusiasts that make a three-day loop up and down the Appalachian Mountains. This has been going on for years, and I was invited to join the group about six years ago. The rule used to be that you had to bring a “classic” car, and in 2021 my 1991 BRG Miata qualified, being over 30 years old. This was a bit of a bitter pill for me to swallow, because it feels like about three years ago that I was looking at clay models of Miatas in the design studio… this is how time compresses exponentially once you age past the half-century mark. Scott C. Requiring classic cars for the tour invites a sort of danger for the group, in that not all the cars might make it home. Particularly for our British and Italian classics, there tends to be a “not going gently into that dark night” decaying halo around the electrical and coolant and braking, etc. systems in these older classic cars. Crankshafts and pistons rarely break, but ancillary support systems such as ignition points and slave cylinders are clearly at risk. Nonetheless, we optimistically pull them out of their garages and put them into a three-day trial-by-fire (well, hopefully not), lest they be labeled “garage queens.” On top of our cockeyed optimism, being members of the Hagerty Driver’s Club with towing privileges emboldens us further. Scott C. One such trip started with two first-generation Miatas (no real risk here), a Porsche 993 (similarly, we can trust new-ish Bosch parts to make the journey), a BMW 3 Series coupe, an old Alfa Romeo Spider, a ‘71 Porsche 911S, and a 1958 Austin Healey Bugeye Sprite that had been thoroughly worked over. Like a middle school dodgeball team, we had a mix of strong and weak players to contend with. Scott C. The trip was to traverse two-lane roads wandering through the Appalachian Mountains where cell coverage was spotty at best. To wit, all of us carried spare parts and tools in anticipation of some sort of roadside episodes. The logic for this game is “if you bring it, you won’t need it,” so mission-critical systems such as fuel and ignition were backed up with NASA-level parts redundancies. Scott C. The Alfa was the first casualty, not even making it out of the hotel parking lot that Saturday morning. Some errant crack in the aged cast aluminum oil pump housing had emerged on the first leg and caused most of the black lubricant to puke itself onto the tarmac overnight while we slumbered. Despite lots of JB Weld and prayers, it was not to be, and time of death was called early Saturday morning. Like soldiers getting ammunition off wounded compatriots, we scavenged the Alfa’s trunk for repair items we might need for the remaining cars. Not polite, but prudent. Scott C. We set off with the remaining fleet, the Alfa driver now resigned to a passenger seat as ballast. The weather was perfect, the roads were clear, and the tour began in earnest. It being Spring, there was a bit of roadkill to contend with and we quickly came up with a metric for ground clearance in the group. The Bugeye was good for one squirrel in the road, but not the average crow. The two Porsches could clear a crow if you winced, but not a possum. The BMW was easily good for a possum but not a fawn, sad as that sight was. Speed through the corners was inversely proportional to the size of the carrion you could straddle, so the Bugeye won that test every time. Our code was to stop at each stop sign or stoplight that involved an actual turn, so as to allow the group, well, to re-group. Between the slight traffic and our individual appetites for aggressive driving (largely within the generous speed limits), this meant that every thirty minutes or so we collapsed the rolling Slinky of cars. As a rule, our tolerance for waiting is around ten minutes. At an average speed of 50 mph, ten minutes equaled just over eight miles, and that is about as far as someone should fall behind. Scott C. As it came to be, one stop lasted fifteen minutes with no sign of our buddy and his six-figure-value ’71 911. Was it off the road due to inertia and bad choices? Had some 50-year-old system failed the owner (brain- or car-related)? Conjectures only lead to stress, so we generally hope for the best and then go looking. As mentioned, there is no cell coverage in most of these areas, which greatly exacerbates any rescue operation. Not only can you not call for mechanical assistance from your friends, but you also can’t call a tow truck. It is like being back in 1971, except that this 911 would have been more reliable back when the Lunar Lander was still under warranty. We sent out our own Donner-party-esque rescue mission: Two of us in separate cars backtracked our route, hoping to not find the 911 in a ditch. These early Porsches are known to be “doctor killers” (as were Beechcraft Bonanzas back in the day) due to very poor “lift throttle” dynamics in fast sweeping corners. The simple trailing arm suspension would cause the outside tire to toe-out on lift throttle engine braking, and the high rear weight bias would slingshot the back of the car off of the road. Experienced 911 pilots developed enlarged anatomical features to be able to keep their gas pedal depressed (no matter how much it spooked their inner core) in a fast corner to keep this demon from pitching them off of the road in a snap-oversteer maneuver. Scott C. After a 20-minute search, we found our friend and his concours-condition jade green 911 safely on the side of the road, all body panels intact, much to our relief. It was the car and thankfully not the driver, that had a self-inflicted wound and needed attention. A quick interview revealed that his alternator light had come on and he had the sense to pull over and wait for help. Since early 911s have a common belt running the alternator and the cooling fan, it would have been foolhardy to try to drive on the battery alone—if it were his belt that had broken, he would have seized his high-compression air-cooled engine in short order. Inspection of the engine revealed that the alternator/fan belt was not connected to the upper pulley, largely because the upper pulley was missing. Its core was still bolted to the common shaft for the fan/alternator, but the outer V-belt pulley rim part was nowhere to be seen. Luckily, air-cooled Porsches have sheet metal all around the engine bay, intended to keep hot undercar air from reaching the cooling fan’s upper intake. This sheet metal has the parallel oft-used function of catching parts that fall off of the top of Porsche engines, in this case catching the shattered perimeter of an aftermarket alternator pulley installed by the previous owner. I cited this failed pulley in an earlier article on the endurance limit of aftermarket parts. We were hundreds of miles from home and repair facilities, and deep out of cell coverage, so towing was not an option. Being on the side of the road in the middle of nowhere in an expensive classic car is a pretty bad situation; you can’t just leave it there overnight unattended. We let the engine cool off as much as ambient temps would allow and gently drove it about a mile to the first spot we could find to park it off of the road. This turned out to be a motel made up of a collection of vacation cabin-ettes, so we found a spot and told the front desk we’d be parking a collector car there for a few hours while we made a repair. Stage one of the fix was underway—the car was safe and we could focus our bandwidth on the repair. Scott C. Back assembled as a group, we put our collective executive skills to work on how to fix this seemingly simple problem. Four of us were degreed engineers, so we were not going to let this be a stumbling block to our weekend tour. Towing the car home was out of the question, as it would be an admission of failure from the get-go. Getting a new pulley was out of the question this far into the boondocks. Somehow, we needed to repair the failed aluminum pulley. One of the more observant non-engineers reminded us that a snow ski resort was just a few miles away, and conjectured that they must have a maintenance shop with some sort of tools that might help. Finding a TIG welder in the boonies is a long shot, but this was a very good plan given our options. A few minutes later, as the sun set over the forests surrounding us, we arrived at the ski resort en masse with the remaining running cars. It was well past skiing season, but we were hoping there was a skeleton crew around. Showing up in an eclectic group of sports cars is a good calling card when you are trying to flush out a car guy in any location. It was easy to find the security guard—because he was a huge man in a small golf cart that looked like a circus act involving a bear. This very large and Sasquatch-ian guard listened to our plight, and with barely a word, quietly led us to a kindred spirit right away at the maintenance shop of this resort. We held the fractured aluminum pieces in front of the mechanic and pleaded our case. Lucky us. I have found over my decades of being around car/airplane/motorcycle guys (and gals) that we all share a certain pluckiness when it comes to solving common mechanical problems. There is some sort of excitement when things break, because you get to fix them, as odd as that sounds. Frankly, without this pluckiness, this hobby would be far too frustrating, since old machines come with their fair share of things to attend to. Scott C. Scott C. Our new friend sadly stated that he did not have a TIG (Tungsten Inert Gas) welder suitable for aluminum welding, and that his MIG (Metal Inert Gas) welder did not have compatible wire for the same, so we were getting nowhere. He did have confidence in brazing it, however, so we reassembled the fractured center hub into the pulley’s outer ring and Dremel-ed it clean. Sadly we did not know what alloy the aftermarket amateurs used for this pulley, but whatever it was it would not accept brazing no matter how hard he worked, skilled as he was. It looked like a dead end. Scott C. Scott C. We started brainstorming about alternate pulleys or pulleys that could be adapted to fit, just to get the car back to our hotel base. After thirty minutes of discussion and silly ideas, the huge-but-silent security guard piped up from the dark back corner of the room and quietly stated that his uncle had two junk Karmann Ghias in his barn. We all looked at each other and smiled. This was to be our path forward; we were certain. There is an old saying in the automotive engineering world: If a German engineer has a problem, he throws 100 years of history at it; if an American engineer has a problem, he throws a $100 at it; if a Japanese engineer has a problem, he throws 100 junior engineers at it; if an Italian engineer has a problem, he goes to lunch… Scott C. Knowing that Porsches and Volkswagens share more than a little DNA (both being originated by Dr. Porsche Sr. himself), there was more than a remote chance that a Karmann Ghia alternator pulley would fit a 911 alternator shaft. Why redesign a shaft once it has proven itself in service—this is a common and useful philosophy in German automaking. A common shaft means a common pulley mounting hub. Our newest friend drove over to his relative’s barn and soon returned with a dusty steel alternator pulley from a mid-seventies Karman Ghia. And, lo and behold, it bolted right up to the Porsche alternator as expected. The belt was not suited for the odd diameter of the VW pulley, and it was O’-dark-thirty by this point, so the next morning we visited a nearby Tractor Supply store to find a wide V belt that was around 2 inches longer in length (the regular auto parts stores didn’t have one wide enough). A bright green John Deere belt turned out to fit perfectly, and the assembly of all of these parts was a thing to behold. Rob S. Scott C. Our friend’s precious 911 was back on the road and continued the tour and even made it through the three-hour trip back home without incident. The correct parts were ordered and installed, and now his high-value car is back to OE levels of reliability, rescued by a broken VW hiding in a barn deep in Appalachia. So, if you ever find yourself in need of a roadside repair for your classic, think out of the box and listen to even the most unlikely solutions—sometimes the answer comes from the quietest corner of the room. Scott C. *** Norman Garrett was the concept engineer for the original Miata back in his days at Mazda’s Southern California Design Studio. When he’s not curating his small collection of dysfunctional automobiles and motorcycles, he teaches automotive engineering classes at UNC Charlotte’s Motorsports Engineering Department in North Carolina. The post When Broken Down in the Boonies, Get Creative and Rely on Community appeared first on Hagerty Media .

title: When to Use CSS if() vs Container Style Queries
summary: Compare CSS if() vs container style queries: when to use each, key syntax traps, range syntax, and 2026 browser support.
body_text: Use the CSS if() function when a single element should decide its own value inline — theming tokens, component states, a responsive property tweak. Reach for a container style query ( @container style(...) ) when one parent’s style should drive a set of rules across multiple descendants. The one-line mental model: if() produces an element-local conditional value; a container style query establishes context, applying conditional rule-blocks from a parent down to its children. Both are conditional-CSS mechanisms that read custom properties, both use the same style() query primitive, and their capabilities overlap enough that picking the wrong one leads to awkward code. This article resolves the overlap: what each does, the mechanical difference that decides which to use, the two syntax gotchas that bite people (semicolons and the colon-vs-equals notation), the range syntax now in both, a scenario-to-tool decision table, and how to ship either one given that browser support is split three ways as of mid-2026. Key Takeaways if() reads custom properties declared in the same rule on the same element and returns one value; @container style() only ever looks upward through the cascade and applies whole rule-blocks to descendants. Inside if() , semicolons (not commas) separate condition–value pairs, and else provides the fallback; with no matching condition and no else , the function returns a guaranteed-invalid value that resolves to the property’s initial value. Inside style() , the colon notation ( style(--n: 3) ) does token/string matching with no math, while the comparison-operator notation ( style(--n = 3) ) parses both sides numerically and evaluates calc() first. As of mid-2026 the support stories diverge: basic container style queries ship in all four major engines (Chrome 111+, Edge 111+, Safari 18+, Firefox 151+), while if() and the enabled-by-default range syntax remain Chromium-only. Because if() is Chromium-only, every if() declaration needs a same-property fallback ahead of it or an @supports guard. What each mechanism is, minimally The if() function is a value-level conditional you place inside any property. Its argument is a semicolon-separated list of condition–value pairs, where each condition is separated from its value by a colon, and an optional else supplies the default: . badge { color : if( style (--variant: danger): white ; style (--variant: muted): # 555 ; else: black ; ); } Each condition is one of three query types: style() tests a custom property on the current element; media() runs an inline media query; supports() runs a feature query. The MDN reference documents all three with the same semicolon grammar — for example, flex-direction: if(media(orientation: landscape): row; else: column;) flips a single property on a media result. A container style query is a @container at-rule whose condition is one or more style() notations reading a containing element’s custom properties. It wraps a block of rules rather than producing a single value: . card { --status: active ; } @container style(--status: active) { . card-title { font-weight : 700 ; } . card-icon { opacity : 1 ; } . card-meta { color : green ; } } Per MDN’s container queries guide , every element is a style container by default — unlike size queries, setting a container-type is not required for style queries. That removes the main setup friction people expect from container queries. The core distinction that decides usage The mechanical difference is scope of lookup. if() reads custom properties declared in the same rule on the same element and is self-contained, while @container style() only ever looks upward through the cascade to an ancestor container. MDN states this directly: using a style query inside if() lets you target an element based on whether a custom property is set on it, rather than checking styles on a parent. The two are explicitly framed as complementary, not redundant. That scope-of-lookup difference has three practical consequences: Output granularity. if() sets exactly one value. @container applies a whole rule-block — multiple declarations across multiple selectors — when its condition is true. As MDN puts it, you can only set single property values with if() style queries, whereas @container queries conditionally apply whole sets of rules. Direction. if() can read a property declared on the very element it’s styling. @container cannot read its own element’s value to style that element; it reads an ancestor’s and styles descendants. Scoping. Only container style queries can scope by container-name . Name a container and the query evaluates only against that container; if the named container doesn’t define the queried property, the block simply doesn’t run. if() has no equivalent scoping control — it always resolves against the element it sits on. So the tiebreaker in the overlap zone is: if one property on one element should flip, if() is less indirection. If several descendants must react to one parent value, @container expresses that with a single condition instead of repeating if() across every child. The syntax gotchas that bite people Semicolons, not commas, separate the pairs in if() . This trips up everyone coming from JavaScript or from comma-separated CSS functions like rgb() . The grammar is if(condition-1: value-1; condition-2: value-2; else: fallback) , with the semicolon after the final pair optional. There must also be no space between if and the opening parenthesis, or the whole declaration is invalid. And when no condition matches and you omitted else , if() returns a guaranteed-invalid value — in a normal property context that resolves to the property’s initial value, which is rarely what you want. Always include else . The colon-vs-equals distinction inside style() is the subtle, high-value detail almost nobody explains. Both if() and container style queries accept two notations with genuinely different behavior, now documented on MDN. The plain (colon) notation does token/string matching of computed values and performs no math. The range (operator) notation — using = , < , <= , > , or >= — resolves each side, parses both as a numeric type, evaluates any calc() , and compares numerically. The consequence, straight from MDN’s own example: . box { --n: calc( 6 / 2 ); } /* FALSE: computed value of --n is the string "calc(6/2)", which is not the token "3" */ @container style(--n: 3) { /* … */ } /* TRUE: both sides parse as <number>, calc(6/2) computes to 3, and 3 = 3 */ @container style(--n = 3) { /* … */ } So style(--n: 3) fails against --n: calc(6/2) , while style(--n = 3) succeeds. Two more rules matter. With the plain notation, the custom-property name must be on the left without var() — style(var(--n): 3) is invalid — whereas the range notation accepts a name, var() , literal, or calc() on either side in any order. And equivalent values (like blue and #0000ff ) only match under the colon notation if the property is registered with @property and a syntax descriptor. The takeaway: use the colon notation for keyword/string matching ( style(--theme: dark) ), and the operator notation for numeric comparison ( style(--columns >= 3) ). Range syntax now lives in both Range syntax extends both mechanisms beyond exact matching to numeric comparison, drawing operands from custom properties, attr() , or literal values. Per the Chrome 142 release notes , a comparison only resolves when both sides resolve to the same data type, limited to seven numeric types: <length> , <number> , <percentage> , <angle> , <time> , <frequency> , and <resolution> . The three-value interval form works too — @container style(0 < --n < 10) — with both comparators pointing the same way. Range syntax is what makes patterns like a notification badge clean. Read a count off an attribute and branch on thresholds: @container style(--count > 99) { . badge :: after { content : " 99+ " ; } } Because the range notation parses numerically, style(--s = new) is false for a keyword like new , while style(--s: new) is true — another reason the notation choice is load-bearing. Which to use, by scenario Scenario Reach for Why Theme token → one property (e.g. color from --theme ) if() One element decides its own value inline Component state flips several child styles (active/error) @container style() One parent value drives a rule-block across descendants Responsive tweak to a single property if() with media() Localized per-property logic; no @media block needed Notification-count badge thresholds Either, via range syntax @container if siblings also react; if() if only the badge changes Contrast-aware text on a themed parent @container style() Children read the parent’s theme and restyle together Feature-gated value (e.g. lch() with fallback) if() with supports() Single value swap on support Multi-property layout change at a breakpoint @media (neither) Both are the wrong tool for large layout shifts The rule of thumb: a single conditional value is an if() job; a conditional context that restyles a subtree is a @container job. Shipping it in 2026 Browser support splits three ways, and the old “conditional CSS is Chromium-only” framing is no longer accurate. Browser support as of June 2026: Feature Chrome / Edge Safari Firefox Container style queries (custom properties, plain syntax) 111+ 18+ 151+ if() function 137+ Not shipped Not shipped Range syntax in style() / if() 142+ (on by default) Not shipped 151, behind layout.css.attr.enabled Basic container style queries are now genuinely cross-engine. They shipped in Chrome and Edge 111, reached WebKit in Safari 18.0 , and arrived in Firefox 151, released May 19, 2026 , which added @container style() query support based on a container’s custom properties. The if() function, by contrast, remains Chromium-only — MDN flags it as experimental with limited availability — and range syntax is enabled by default only in Chromium. Firefox 151 ships @container style() range syntax but disabled by default, behind the layout.css.attr.enabled preference. The practical upshot: if() does not gracefully degrade, so write a default declaration first and let supporting browsers override it, or wrap the rule in an @supports guard. One pattern covers both mechanisms: /* fallback first — every browser applies this */ . card-title { font-weight : 400 ; } /* progressive enhancement: only style-query-capable engines apply this */ @supports ( container-type : normal ) { @container style(--status: active) { . card-title { font-weight : 700 ; } } } /* if(): static value first, then the conditional override */ . badge { padding : 0.25em ; } . badge { padding : if( style (--size: lg): 0.5em ; else: 0.25em ); } Because if() and default-on range syntax still render down their fallback path in Firefox and Safari — browsers a Chrome-using developer rarely opens during development — cross-browser session replay is a useful technique for actually watching the fallback branch render on a real user’s browser rather than assuming it looks right. Pick by intent, not novelty: a conditional value on one element is if() ; a conditional context that restyles a subtree from a parent is a container style query. Ship either behind a fallback today, re-check the support matrix before you rely on if() in production, and the two will increasingly cover the conditional-CSS space that once required custom-property hacks and JavaScript. FAQs Can container style queries read the same element's own custom property, like if() can? No. A container style query always looks upward through the cascade to an ancestor container and applies its rules to descendants, so it cannot read a custom property on the very element it would style. The if() function is the opposite: it reads custom properties declared in the same rule on the same element and resolves a value inline. If you need an element to branch on its own property, use if(); if a parent's value should restyle its children, use a container style query. Do container style queries require setting a container-type, the way size queries do? No. Every element is a style container by default, so style queries on custom properties work without declaring container-type. This differs from container size queries, which do require container-type (such as inline-size) on the queried ancestor before any size condition can resolve. This is documented on MDN's container queries guide, and it removes the main setup step developers expect when first reaching for the @container at-rule. Why does my style query with calc() never match? Because the plain colon notation does token and string matching with no math. A property set to calc(6 / 2) computes to the string 'calc(6/2)', which never matches the token 3, so style(--n: 3) returns false. To compare numerically, use the comparison-operator notation, style(--n = 3), which resolves each side, evaluates calc(), parses both as a numeric type, and compares numerically, so it returns true. Use the colon form for keyword matching and the operator form for numeric comparison. Does if() degrade gracefully in Safari and Firefox? No. As of mid-2026 if() ships only in Chromium browsers (Chrome and Edge 137+), so Safari and Firefox ignore any declaration containing it and fall back to whatever value applied before. Write a static default declaration first and let supporting browsers override it, or wrap the conditional rule in an @supports guard. Basic container style queries are safer cross-engine, shipping in Chrome 111+, Edge 111+, Safari 18+, and Firefox 151+, but the enabled-by-default range syntax remains Chromium-only.
